**ChalkTalk Design Document**

# Overview

ChalkTalk is an interactive class collaboration platform modeled after Piazza. Instructors can create classes that students join. Instructors post announcements, while students ask questions and get responses from instructors or teaching assistants.

# Functional Requirements

### **Account Creation and Management**

To create an account, an email and a password are required. OAuth is also supported. Upon registration, an email is sent to the provided email to verify the account. Passwords must meet minimum length and complexity requirements.

Passwords can be modified by the user; a new password must meet the same requirements. If a user forgets their password, a reset email is sent, allowing them to set a new one.

Accounts can be deleted at any time.

### **Classes**

Users can create classes, which function as independent, isolated forums. When a class is created, the creating user becomes the instructor of that class.

Classes can be archived or deleted. Archiving a class makes it read-only, preventing new posts, replies, and new users from joining. When a class is deleted, all data stored under the class is deleted.

### **Posts**

Users can create posts on the main page. There are three types of posts: questions, notes, and polls.

Questions can be marked as duplicates by an instructor or TA, who refers to a canonical post. When this happens, the student who posted the question will be notified via email and the post will be hidden, redirecting the post link to the canonical post. The duplicate question will be hidden, but can be managed by instructor or TA’s via a duplicate posts menu where they can also be reverted.

###  **Questions**

Questions can be posted by any user. When a user creates a question, similar existing posts are surfaced automatically. Any user may respond, creating a collaborative response: either the instructors' response or the students' response. If a TA or instructor responds, it becomes the instructors' response and may be edited by TAs and instructors. If a student responds, it becomes the students' response and may be edited by students.

Responses can be endorsed by a TA or instructor. Once endorsed, a response can no longer be edited.

Followups can be posted in response to answers, and followups can themselves be responded to, forming a nested structure.

### **Notes**

Notes can be posted by any user. Responses cannot be posted to notes.

### **Polls**

Polls can be posted by instructors or TAs. A poll contains a list of options that any user can vote on. Polls cannot be responded to.

Posts, responses, and followups support LaTeX and Markdown formatting, as well as image and document upload.

Posts, responses, and followups each have an author and timestamp; timestamps update on edit. Collaborative responses record every user who has edited them.

Users can mark individual posts, responses, or followups as anonymous. When marked anonymous, the author is displayed as "Anonymous" to other students, while remaining visible to TAs and instructors.

### **Channels**

A channel is a group of discussion spaces called subchannels. Channels can only be created by instructors and TAs, and contain a title and description. Subchannels can be created by any user and contain a title and introductory message.

Channels can be manually archived or deleted by an instructor or TA. When archived, all subchannels become read-only and new subchannels cannot be created. Channels are automatically archived after a configurable period of inactivity, defined as no new subchannels being created and no new activity within any subchannel.

### **Search**

Posts are indexed for full-text and fuzzy search, with results ranked so that titles, endorsed answers, and more recent activity are weighted more heavily. Results can be filtered by tag, author, date range, and answered/unanswered status.

When a user drafts a new question, related existing posts are surfaced live, using the same underlying search index. Any user can mark a post as a duplicate of another; a TA or instructor can confirm the merge, consolidating engagement onto the canonical post.

### **Course Resources**

Instructors can upload or link resources relating to the course, such as syllabus documents, lecture notes, assignments, course policies, and external links.

Uploaded documents can be divided into instructor-defined regions, such as a diagram or paragraph on a given page. Each region is independently searchable and can be directly linked to from posts, responses, and followups. Text within a defined region is extracted via OCR to support search.

### **Live Collaborative Sessions**

Any user can start a live, shared code editor session, linked to a post or channel, for use during office hours or collaborative debugging. Multiple participants can edit the same session concurrently, with changes merging in real time without conflict.

### **Statistics**

Course statistics are compiled per course in a statistics tab. These statistics include:

* Daily activity

* Questions and answers per student

* Posts viewed

* Average response time

Response time is defined as the time between when a question is posted and when an endorsed answer is posted in response.

### **Knowledge Surfacing**

The system tracks engagement signals per post, including view count, followup activity, and edits made to endorsed answers after initial endorsement, in order to identify content likely to be broadly relevant to the class. Surfaced content is displayed in a per-course digest view, and instructors can also manually pin content to this digest.

### **Role Permissions**

| Action | Student | TA | Instructor |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Create question/note | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Create poll | No | Yes | Yes |
| Create announcement | No | Yes/no | Yes |
| Endorse answers | No | Yes | Yes |
| Archive/delete post | Own only | Yes | Yes |
| Create channel | No | Yes | Yes |
| Manage members | No | Maybe | Yes |
| Archive/delete class | No | No | Yes |

# Nonfunctional Requirements

### **Security**

All endpoints will be TLS encrypted. User passwords will be hashed using bcrypt. To enforce per-tenant isolation, the database will have row-level security, only displaying data for courses that the user is in.

### **Failure Handling**

In the presence of errors, generic error messages will be displayed to the user to hide system internals. If an error occurs with a database write operation, any preceding writes will be rolled back to preserve database integrity.

### **Performance and Scalability**

All API requests must have a latency below or at 200 ms. When CPU load goes above 60%, new web server instances will be automatically provisioned.

### **Metrics and Logging**

System and infrastructure metrics will be collected every 60 seconds. Results from all API requests and responses will be logged and retained for 1 year.

# Architecture

### **Core Architecture**

The system consists of a frontend, a backend made up of three processes (a web server, a collaboration engine, and a background worker), a PostgreSQL database, an object store, and an email provider.

**Frontend.** The frontend is a React application built with Vite. It communicates with the backend in two ways. Standard requests, such as loading posts, creating a question, or voting in a poll, go to the web server as JSON over HTTPS. Live editing sessions connect to the collaboration engine over a WebSocket.

**Web server.** The web server is an Express.js REST API and handles most of the application logic. It validates sessions and CSRF tokens, checks each user's role in the course, and reads and writes course data in PostgreSQL. It also uploads and fetches images and documents in the object store. When a request needs slow work, such as OCR or sending an email, the web server adds a job to a queue table in PostgreSQL instead of doing the work during the request.

**Collaboration engine.** The collaboration engine is a Hocuspocus server that holds active Yjs documents in memory. Clients send edits to it over a WebSocket, and it merges them and broadcasts them to everyone else in the same session. Before accepting a connection, it validates a one-use ticket issued by the web server. It loads each document from PostgreSQL when the first participant joins and saves the merged state back periodically.

**Worker.** The worker is a separate Node.js process that claims queued jobs from PostgreSQL and runs them. Jobs include OCR on uploaded documents, which the worker reads from the object store, digest generation, and sending email. Because the queue is stored in the database, queued jobs aren't lost if the worker restarts.

**PostgreSQL.** PostgreSQL stores users, courses, memberships, posts, sessions, the job queue, and saved collaboration documents. Row-level security limits every query to the courses the current user belongs to.

**Object store.** The object store holds uploaded images and documents. It is AWS S3 in the managed deployment and SeaweedFS in the self-hosted deployment. Both use the same S3 API, so the application code is identical in both.

**Email provider.** The email provider delivers verification, password reset, and notification emails. It is AWS SES in the managed deployment and any SMTP server in the self-hosted deployment. Only the worker sends email.

# Deployment

Because ChalkTalk offers both a managed cloud deployment and a self-managed deployment, the implementation and hosting of some services differ between the two versions. In the managed deployment, the React frontend is deployed to Vercel. The web server, background worker, and collaboration engine run on AWS ECS. PostgreSQL is provided by AWS RDS, AWS S3 provides object storage, and AWS SES provides email delivery. In the self-managed deployment, the frontend and backend components run as containers managed through Docker Compose. The deployment includes PostgreSQL for application data and durable jobs, SeaweedFS for S3-compatible object storage, and a configurable SMTP server for email delivery.

### **AI module**

AI features,  such as AI responses to student questions, are accessed through a single AI provider interface in the backend, so the rest of the system never calls a specific AI service directly. The web server uses it for requests that need an immediate response, and the worker uses it for slower tasks such as generating embeddings for new posts. Each deployment selects one of three modes through configuration:

* No AI: AI features are hidden, and search uses PostgreSQL full-text search only. ChalkTalk remains fully functional in this mode, which is the default for self-hosted instances.
* Bring your own key (BYOK): The instance calls a hosted AI provider using an API key supplied by the operator and stored as a server-side secret. In the managed deployment, the ChalkTalk team provides this key; in a self-hosted deployment, the administrator supplies their own.
* Local model: The instance calls a model running on the operator's own hardware through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model can run as an additional container in the Docker Compose deployment, so no data leaves the self-hoster's infrastructure.

In the managed deployment, system metrics and request logs are collected with AWS CloudWatch, which covers the 60-second metrics interval and one-year log retention in the nonfunctional requirements.

### **Background jobs**

 Slow or non-request-critical work is delegated to a background worker process. This work  includes:

*  OCR and text extraction from documents
*  Digest generation
*  Email delivery

 The web server or scheduler queues a job by inserting a record into PostgreSQL with a queued status. Database storage ensures that queued work survives application and worker restarts.

  When the worker claims a job, it marks the record as running. After completing the work, it marks the job as successful. If processing fails temporarily, the job is returned to the queue for another attempt. Jobs  that exceed their retry limit are marked as dead. Completed job records are removed later by scheduled retention cleanup.

### **Concurrent editing**

Concurrent editing of questions and answers is handled by Yjs and Hocuspocus. Each collaboratively editable question or answer has its own Yjs document. When a user edits the content, Yjs immediately applies the change to the local document and encodes it as a CRDT update. The Hocuspocus provider  then sends the update to the Hocuspocus server over an authenticated WebSocket connection. The server applies the update to its shared Yjs document and broadcasts it to the other connected clients. Each client merges the received updates deterministically, allowing every client to converge on the same document state. Finally, Hocuspocus  authenticates connections, loads the saved Yjs state from PostgreSQL, and periodically persists the updated document state using debounced writes.

### **Duplicate Post Management**

### **Authentication, authorization, and session management**

ChalkTalk uses cookie-based, server-side sessions for authentication. When a user successfully logs in with an email address and password, the server creates a session in PostgreSQL. It stores a hash of a randomly generated session credential and returns that credential in a secure, HttpOnly cookie. The server also returns a CSRF token associated with the session. The browser automatically includes the session cookie with authenticated requests. The server uses the credential to retrieve the active session and identify the user. For authenticated POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests, the frontend also supplies the CSRF token in the X-CSRF-Token header. This prevents another website from using the browser’s session cookie to perform unauthorized actions.

Authorization is performed separately for each operation. The server retrieves the user’s course membership and determines whether their role—student, teaching assistant, or instructor—permits the requested  action. The request is accepted only when both the session and the required authorization are valid.

# Data Model

### **Accounts, courses, and membership**

![][image2]

An organization represents a school and is identified by its email domain, and every user belongs to exactly one organization. Organizations own courses. Course memberships connect users to courses and store each user's role in that course, so the same person can be a student in one course and a TA in another. Sessions store hashed session credentials and CSRF tokens for logged-in users. Email verification tokens are keyed on email instead of user ID, because verification happens before the account exists, while password reset tokens belong to an existing user. Idempotency records let a client safely retry a create request without creating duplicates, and rate limit buckets count recent attempts so login, signup, and email requests can be throttled.

### **Posts and discussion**

![][image3]

A single posts table holds questions, notes, and polls, with a type column telling them apart. A post can point to another post as its duplicate. Poll options and poll votes are only used by poll posts. Answers only belong to question posts, and each question has at most one student answer and one staff answer, marked by kind. Answer contributors record every user who has edited a collaborative answer. Followups belong to an answer and can point to a parent followup, which is how nested replies are stored. Tags are defined per course and linked to posts through post\_tags. Attachments can belong to a post, answer, followup, or message, tracked with a foreign key. The file itself lives in the object store, and the row only keeps a reference to it.

### **Channels, resources, and live collaboration**

## ![][image4]

Channels contain subchannels, which contain messages. Resources are course materials such as the syllabus or lecture notes. An instructor can divide an uploaded resource into regions, and the text in each region is extracted with OCR so it can be searched. A collaboration session is a live editing session tied to either a post or a subchannel. Each session has one collaboration document, which stores the binary Yjs state. Before a user can connect to a session over WebSocket, they request a short-lived, one-use connection ticket, which is tied to both the session and their login session. The jobs table is the queue for the background worker. It doesn't reference other tables directly because each job's details are stored in its payload.

### **Tenant isolation**

Every table that holds course content has a course\_id column, even when the course could be found through a parent row. For example, followups stores course\_id directly instead of reaching it through answers and then posts. This keeps row-level security simple: every course-scoped table uses the same policy, which only returns rows whose course\_id belongs to a course the current user is a member of. It also makes the tenant-isolation test straightforward, since the test can query any content table as a user from one course and check that no rows from another course come back.

### **Single-tenant self-hosted mode**

The self-hosted deployment uses exactly the same schema as the managed deployment. A self-hosted instance usually has a single organization for its school's email domain, and it can start with one course and add more later. Nothing in the schema changes: the organization and course\_id columns still exist, they just only have one value. Because both deployments share the same schema, migrations, row-level security policies, and tests work the same way in both.

# Key Flows

![][image5]

## Key Flow: Posting a Question

While the student types a title and body, the frontend waits for a short pause in typing and then sends the current draft to the web server as a search query (`GET /api/v1/courses/{courseId}/posts?q=…&type=question`). Waiting for a pause keeps the frontend from sending a request on every keystroke. The web server checks the student's session and course membership, then runs a ranked full-text search in PostgreSQL. The search is limited to the student's course and weights titles, endorsed answers, and recent activity more heavily. The top matches are shown in a related-questions panel next to the draft, and this repeats as the student keeps typing.

If a related post already answers the question, the student can open it and no new post is created, which is the main way ChalkTalk cuts down on duplicate questions. Otherwise, the student submits the question. The frontend sends a `POST` request with the session's CSRF token and an idempotency key, so retrying after a network error can't create a duplicate post. The web server checks the session, CSRF token, the student's role, and that the course isn't archived. It then inserts the post, its search vector, and the idempotency key in a single database transaction. Because the search vector is written in the same transaction as the post, the new question is searchable right away, so the next student drafting a similar question will see it in their related-questions panel.

# Testing

All API’s will be unit tested, mocking external dependencies. Integration testing will validate full flows that rely on end to end dependencies, such as authentication and concurrent edits.

# Tradeoffs

### **Server-based vs Serverless Architecture**

Function-based serverless platforms can simplify provisioning and infrastructure management, but they are a poor fit for ChalkTalk’s collaboration engine. Hocuspocus runs as a long-lived WebSocket server that keeps active Yjs documents in memory, authenticates participants, distributes Yjs updates, and coordinates persistence. Implementing this behavior with short-lived functions would require additional services for connection management and shared state. Because collaborative editing is a core part of ChalkTalk, the managed backend is deployed as long-running containers on AWS ECS.

### **Caching**

ChalkTalk will not initially include a dedicated caching layer. At the expected application scale, PostgreSQL should provide adequate performance, while Redis would introduce additional deployment, cache-invalidation, and consistency complexity without a demonstrated need. API latency, database utilization, connection saturation, and slow queries will be monitored. If the application exceeds its latency targets and profiling identifies repeated database reads as the cause, Redis may be introduced selectively for suitable read-heavy data.

### **Dedicated Vector Database**

 At the current application scale, a dedicated vector database such as Pinecone is unnecessary. If semantic search is introduced, an embedding model will generate vector embeddings, while PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension will store them and perform similarity searches. Keeping vector and relational data in PostgreSQL reduces operational complexity and allows course permissions and metadata filters to be applied within the same database queries. A dedicated vector database will be considered only if profiling shows that the volume or throughput exceeds PostgreSQL’s capabilities.

### **Relational vs. Nonrelational Database**

ChalkTalk’s data is highly relational. Users belong to organizations and courses, while courses contain memberships, channels, posts, answers, resources, and collaboration records. These relationships require  joins, transactions, foreign keys, and consistency constraints, making PostgreSQL a strong fit. At the application’s expected scale, horizontal partitioning is unnecessary. PostgreSQL can initially be scaled by optimizing queries and indexes, adjusting database resources, and tuning connection pooling. More complex scaling strategies should be considered only if observed usage exceeds the capacity of a single database instance.
